overview: Sarmates is this map’s name for Sarmatian peoples, a varied Iranian-speaking world associated with the Pontic-Caspian steppe. The imported outline for 100 to 1 BCE is an approximate regional label, not the frontier of a single state. Earlier Lower Volga evidence and later communities in Hungary and Roman Britain are identified separately below; neither the people nor their history stopped at the map’s endpoint.

periods.title: Lower Don communities
periods.summary: Burials and imported objects help date Sarmatian activity before and during the map’s first-century BCE window.

periods.title: Later westward connections
periods.summary: Sarmatian communities, cavalry units and farming villages remained important in the Roman period.

sections.title: Everyday belongings and the people behind them

items.text: Dating Sarmatian arrivals in the Lower Don is an archaeological puzzle. A stamped Rhodian amphora, black-glazed drinking cups and molded bowls helped Glebov and Dedyulkin place some early complexes in the middle decades of the second century BCE. Imported containers can act as time clues when a grave has no written date.

Lower Don graves of the second and first centuries BCE contain large metal mirrors with raised rims and projecting handles, as well as smaller flat disks without handles. Many retained traces of cases; one had a stand. Looking at your reflection could involve a carefully protected portable object rather than a bathroom wall.

Only about a fifth of the mirrors in that study survived whole. Some were cut, bent or broken, and the author interprets much of this damage as part of funerary rituals. A broken mirror in a grave therefore need not mean its owner was simply careless with their belongings.

An earlier Lower Volga study examined fifty-eight children and adolescents from burials dated 400 to 100 BCE. Researchers recorded dental tartar, including deposits on baby teeth, and one case of tooth decay in a teenager. Such small traces let children enter a history often dominated by warriors and wealthy adults.

sections.title: A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace

items.text: At Sadovy Kurgan near Novocherkassk, excavated in 1962, a burial lay in a rectangular pit beneath wooden planks and reeds. Scholarly discussion places the assemblage broadly in the first century BCE. Although robbers had entered the grave, equipment deposited around it still preserved traces of the funeral gathering.

Two bronze cauldrons at Sadovy were blackened with soot. The excavator connected them with cooking for the funeral feast. Eight silver bowls had been stacked upside down and covered with a larger silver vessel. Even a lavish ceremony involved the practical business of cooking and gathering the dishes together.

Sadovy’s large decorative roundels were made from hammered silver covered in gold leaf. Griffins and feline animals filled their surfaces. Thin precious layers could create a brilliant effect without making every part solid gold. Their construction records the work of specialists in shaping, covering and joining metal.

A later gold collar from Khokhlach, another burial mound near Novocherkassk, belongs to the first century CE. It had three joined rings, turquoise settings and pairs of facing lions. The Metropolitan Museum’s example is a nineteenth-century electrotype copy; the ancient original is in the Hermitage. The distinction matters when following an object’s story.

sections.title: Later villages and a real written message

items.text: Centuries later and west of this map’s outline, Sarmatian communities farmed on the Great Hungarian Plain. At Rákóczifalva-Bagi-földek, fourth- and fifth-century CE plant remains emphasize cereals, while animal remains are dominated by cattle. These villagers combined crops and livestock in a landscape of fields, grassland, floodplain woods and river.

At the same Hungarian site, researchers identified twelve grape pips from four pits. They suggest contacts with Roman food traditions and possibly food exchange with Roman provinces. A few seeds can raise interesting questions about meals, but they do not establish that every household owned a vineyard.

Writing sample: “DEO SAN” opens a stone inscription from Ribchester in Britain dated 31 August 241 CE. Expanded as “Deo sancto,” it means “To the holy god.” The dedication concerns Apollo Maponus and a Sarmatian cavalry unit. This later Roman military text is Latin, not an example of the Sarmatians’ own language.

The same inscription names Aelius Antoninus, a Roman officer from Melitene near the Euphrates. His dedication links an officer from the eastern empire, a unit carrying a Sarmatian name and a fort in Britain. The surviving stone is part of a monument’s pedestal, with a relief of Apollo beside the text.

ending.text: There was no single Sarmatian state to fall in 1 BCE. Communities continued through the Roman centuries. Later Hunnic expansion broke up Alanic political alliances within this wider world, while different groups moved, joined new coalitions or continued in regions such as the Caucasus. Political labels and communities changed along different paths.
